current_episode.title: Greg Kelly - AMK Hardware & Entrance Composite Door Solutions

guest.entreprise: AMK Hardware & Entrance Composite Door Solutions
guest.bio_context: Greg Kelly was born into the hardware business—his father started a hardware distributor in Northern Ireland in 1980, initially supplying everything from wheelbarrows to PVC components, eventually becoming a main distributor for brands like Hoppy and OGU. Greg joined the family business in 2000 after university, starting in telesales and progressively moving into sales leadership. He led the company's expansion into composite door manufacturing, initially through prep slabs and components in the early 2000s, then into full door set production starting around 2017-2018. Today he oversees 58 staff across three sites (two in UK and one in Ireland) and manages both the legacy hardware distribution and the composite door manufacturing division.

pending_qa.q: What operational challenges emerged when composite door demand suddenly increased during COVID-19?
pending_qa.r: Before COVID, the business was producing 10-15 door sets per week using spreadsheets and T-card systems. Upon reopening, orders jumped to 60-80 door sets per week, and simultaneously the prep slab business became very busy. Kelly admits they had no processes in place for that level of growth, lacked proper staffing, let customers down, burned bridges with some clients, and had supplier issues. This forced them to step back and completely rebuild their manufacturing processes, systems, and team structure to handle future growth properly.

pending_qa.q: What defines the quality approach of a boutique composite door manufacturer competing against larger volume producers?
pending_qa.r: Kelly emphasizes they do not chase volume and never source cheap components just to win orders. They position themselves in the middle market—not the cheapest, not the most expensive—offering doors ranging from £600 to £2,000, all made with components they believe are the best for each application. They add finishing touches like recessing Inox cassettes into doors rather than surface-mounting them, painting the hinge side to match the face color, and offering non-standard options like Oswald George and Bars. The focus is on delivering a product Kelly would put in his own house and providing personalized service rather than pursuing numbers-driven growth.

pending_qa.q: How does supplier loyalty influence a composite door manufacturer's product choices and relationships?
pending_qa.r: Kelly states they use Winkhouse Locks exclusively on all products because of a very good relationship built through their hardware business agency in Ireland, despite being approached by other lock manufacturers. The relationship matters as much as the product itself—it extends to furniture, door slabs, and glass sourcing. He emphasizes that working with suppliers daily means 'you might as well spend it with somebody you've got a relationship with' rather than constantly chasing the cheapest price option.

pending_qa.q: What role does remote family business structure play in day-to-day management across geographically separated sites?
pending_qa.r: The business operates with 58 staff across three sites—two in the UK (one in Nottingham/Alfredon area, one new facility) and one in Lurgan, Northern Ireland—with Kelly managing from Northern Ireland but traveling frequently to the UK operation. He emphasizes the importance of having trustworthy staff who can operate independently and having full digital connectivity to all systems. The Lurgan office handles all accounting and purchasing for both locations. Kelly notes this requires good communication and understanding that a remote manager can place extra pressure on local management teams, but he remains hands-on, willing to step onto the production floor to resolve quality issues or help customers.

pending_qa.q: How did a small regional warehouse location in Alfredon become the strategic UK base for a national composite door distributor?
pending_qa.r: When Kelly's father decided to expand the business from Northern Ireland to the UK mainland in 1992, the location choice was entirely opportunistic rather than strategic—an employee lived in Alfredon and needed a warehouse nearby. However, the area proved advantageous: it offered good motorway links for distribution, had a manufacturing base nearby (they supplied profile companies like Sincere and Shearframe), and had existing customer relationships from the hardware side. This accidental choice turned out to be well-positioned geographically for serving the broader UK market.
